extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency policymakers, judges, and researchers working on algorithmic governance and notice-and-comment issues
extracted.subtask_description: Framework for determining when an agency-deployed algorithm is "practically binding" (and therefore functionally a rule subject to the APA notice-and-comment process), emphasizing ex ante structural factors and their empirical/theoretical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative factor analysis for 'practically binding'
rubrics_metrics.description: None of the factors we discuss is independently necessary for finding an algorithm to be a rule. Rather, an accumulation of factors increases the probability that an algorithm is 'practically binding' and thus subject to the notice and comment process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat any single factor as dispositive; evaluate multiple structural and contextual indicators together. Courts should weigh an accumulation of ex ante and ex post factors (e.g., signal structure, costs of deviation, access to auxiliary evidence) to assess whether the algorithm will be persuasive enough in practice to function as a rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of access to auxiliary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A critical variable is the degree to which an adjudicator can easily access auxiliary evidence against which the algorithm’s prediction may be evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If auxiliary evidence (factual record, country-of-origin data, freeform descriptions) is seamless to access and clearly structured, adjudicators are more likely to exercise discretion and less likely to defer. Empirical example: child maltreatment hotline where UI access to underlying records enabled users to detect erroneous scores. Theoretical support: lower cost to acquire information decreases sender's power (Matysková & Montes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of bare predictions without supporting information
rubrics_metrics.description: When an adjudicator simply receives a bare risk score with no access to other information, a rational decision-maker has no room for deliberation and must rely completely on the prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bare scores increase the likelihood the algorithm will be practically binding. Assess whether the system supplies only a bottom-line metric or also supplies underlying evidence; lack of other signals indicates absence of discretion and stronger rule-like effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: User interface design that surfaces underlying information
rubrics_metrics.description: The user interface’s ease of access to underlying information about each case can prevent blind reliance on algorithmic recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate UI affordances: whether users can quickly view referral calls, administrative records, inputs used in risk calculation, or other supporting evidence. Good UI that surfaces auxiliary signals can overcome even modest costs of deviation (e.g., managerial approval) and reduce automation bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of deviation imposed on decisionmakers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the agency places a cost on disagreement with the algorithm’s recommendation (e.g., requiring manager approval, requiring written reasons, risking employment consequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher costs of deviation make line officers less likely to override recommendations and increase the algorithm’s rule-like character. Examples: ICE requirement to provide reasons for disagreement; White House approval requirement for drone strikes above a CDE threshold. But costs interact with other factors (ease of auxiliary evidence, incentives) and do not uniformly produce blind compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance strategies and costs on accepting recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some types of resistance strategies (e.g., imposing costs on acceptance rather than on deviation, or stochastic/randomized oversight) can encourage more scrutiny of the signal and reduce blind compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The persuasion literature shows that requiring reports or costs on a random subset of acceptances can increase informativeness and receivers’ payoffs. Assess whether agency procedures place burdens on accepting recommendations (rather than on dissent), which can motivate officers to verify signals rather than rubber-stamp them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perverse incentives and gaming caused by system thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Making noncompliance costly may lead actors to sidestep prescribed procedures or game inputs to avoid costs (e.g., tweak payload to keep casualty estimates below a threshold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for design features or thresholds that create incentives to manipulate inputs or behaviors to avoid oversight obligations. Such gaming shows the system is shaping behavior in practice and can indicate a rule-like effect even if formal discretion remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of the signal: bottom-line recommendation versus evidentiary inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms that give a bottom-line recommended action (e.g., recommended bail) are more persuasive than models that identify relevant factors or offer reasons without drawing a bottom-line conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the algorithm issues a definitive recommended outcome or merely surfaces evidence/citations/inputs. Systems that recommend inputs (research-assistant role) leave more reasoning steps to the adjudicator and are less likely to be treated as APA rules; bottom-line recommendations increase anchoring and deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explainability, complexity, and presentation of explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence, quality, amount, and complexity of explanations affect how persuasive an algorithm is — sometimes in counterintuitive ways (e.g., too much transparency can increase complacency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider empirical HCI findings: simplified explanations can decrease deference and automation bias, whereas excessive detail or high transparency can overwhelm users and create out-of-the-loop complacency. Evaluate design choices about explanation granularity and presentation modality when assessing practical bindingness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veracity and quality of explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: High-veracity (accurate, truthful) explanations tend to push users toward correct answers; inaccurate (low-veracity) explanations can induce disagreement even when the recommendation is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether explanations are reliable and verifiable. Low-veracity explanations can undermine trust and lead to corrective behavior, while high-quality explanations may increase compliance and reduce error detection—so judges should weigh explanation quality when inferring bindingness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchoring effects of presenting final recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing a model’s bottom-line recommendation may create an anchoring effect that causes users to accept the model’s judgment regardless of correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the system displays a final recommendation alongside explanations; removing the final recommendation (only suggesting relevant inputs) may reduce human dependence and preserve discretion. Consider empirical evidence that explanations plus a bottom-line increase acceptance even for incorrect predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability and cost to detect algorithmic mistakes (lie-detection capability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The receiver’s (adjudicator’s) capability and cost to detect mistakes in the algorithm influence whether humans will catch algorithm errors and thus whether the system will be binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the cost of detecting mistakes is low and lie-detection is sufficiently reliable, receiver performance improves and reliance decreases. Conversely, if detection is costly or users are inexperienced, over-reliance and rule-like effects are more likely. Consider empirical/theoretical results on lie detection and human expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of legally required information by the algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms that fail to incorporate legally required information can lead to arbitrary decisions when humans over-rely on them (e.g., RCA failing to consider detainee vulnerabilities or age).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the algorithm’s input set or design excludes information that statutes or case law require be considered. Judicial cases (Fraihat, Ramirez) show that exclusion of required factors can produce viable APA/constitutional claims and indicate that algorithmic reliance produced practically binding, defective decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal characteristics of adjudicators affecting deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Users’ self-confidence, experience, and other personal characteristics influence their likelihood of deferring to algorithmic recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating bindingness, consider heterogeneity among decisionmakers: inexperienced or low-confidence officers are more likely to over-rely, while experienced or confident officers may better detect errors. Because agency procedures often cannot be conditioned on staff identity, consider system design that mitigates deference across user types.
